name: Worship of the Jina image (jina-pūjā)
method_summary: The householder bathes the consecrated image and offers eight substances — water, sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamp, unbroken rice, sweets and fruit (the aṣṭaprakārī pūjā) — with verses recalling the Jina's qualities, followed by inner worship (caityavandana, praise, meditation). The Digambara Terāpantha offers only non-living, dry substances; mendicants perform only inner worship. The Jina, being liberated, does not respond; the worshipper is purified by recalling his qualities.

warnings.text: Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs reject material worship because it harms one-sensed beings (water, flowers, fire); Mūrtipūjaka teachers restrict material worship to householders.

equivalents.note: outwardly similar image worship, but the Jina is not a grace-giving deity and receives nothing

name: The bathing rite (snātra-pūjā)
method_summary: A congregational re-enactment of Indra's bathing of the newborn Tīrthaṅkara on Mount Meru: a small image is bathed with water and other substances to hymns, recalling the birth-kalyāṇaka.

name: Veneration of the Jina (caityavandana)
method_summary: A liturgy of salutation before the image or a representation of the Jina, with prostrations, the Śakrastava ('namo'tthu ṇaṃ') and hymns; Haribhadra's Lalitavistarā comments on it.

name: Paryuṣaṇa
method_summary: An eight-day period at the height of the rains (Bhādrapada) of fasting according to capacity, daily confession, listening to sermons and, among Mūrtipūjakas, the public reading of the Kalpa Sūtra (the Prakrit text alone on the last day), ending with the annual confession (Saṃvatsarī) and asking forgiveness of all.
duration: eight days (Digambaras: ten days, Das Lakṣaṇa)

warnings.text: One who does not forgive and ask forgiveness is not a true follower of the discipline: 'the essence of monkhood is calm'.

name: Public reading of the Kalpa Sūtra
method_summary: During Paryuṣaṇa a mendicant reads and explains the Kalpa Sūtra (with the Subodhikā or similar commentary) to the congregation over several days; the reading of Mahāvīra's birth, with the display of the fourteen dreams, is a festive high point; on Saṃvatsarī the Prakrit 'Bārasa Sūtra' is recited.

name: Das Lakṣaṇa Parva
method_summary: Ten days of the Digambara rains festival, each devoted to one of the ten dharmas (supreme forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, purity, truth, restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possession, chastity), with readings of the Tattvārthasūtra, worship and fasting according to capacity, ending with forgiveness.

name: The annual confession (saṃvatsarī pratikramaṇa)
method_summary: The longest form of confession, performed on the last day of Paryuṣaṇa: reviewing the year's transgressions against beings and vows, repenting with 'micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ', and asking forgiveness of all living beings and of each person one has wronged.

equivalents.note: the annual form of the daily and fortnightly confession

name: The rainy-season retreat (cāturmāsa)
method_summary: Mendicants stop wandering for the four months of the rains and stay in one place chosen with the local community, to avoid harming the many beings that appear; it is a season of teaching, study and austerity.

name: Wandering on foot (vihāra)
method_summary: Outside the rains, mendicants travel on foot only, never in vehicles, staying a limited time in any place, watching the ground to avoid harming beings (the carefulness in walking).

name: The alms-round (gocarī)
method_summary: The mendicant goes from house to house taking a little food 'like a bee from flowers', accepting only what was not prepared for him and is free of the faults of alms; Śvetāmbara mendicants collect in bowls and eat in their lodging; the Digambara monk eats once a day, standing, from his cupped hands, at a house where he is ceremonially received.

name: Plucking out the hair (keśa-loca)
method_summary: At initiation and periodically thereafter (for Digambara monks every two to four months) the mendicant's hair and beard are plucked out by hand, as an exercise of endurance and detachment from the body.

name: Initiation into mendicancy (dīkṣā)
method_summary: The candidate, with family consent, renounces possessions in a public ceremony, receives the mendicant's equipment (whisk, bowls or water-pot) and a new name, takes the vow of equanimity for life, and has the hair plucked; Śvetāmbaras later confer the 'great initiation' (chedopasthāpanā) with the five vows; Digambara men become naked monks after the stages of kṣullaka and ailaka.

name: The fourfold accomplishment (ārādhanā) at life's end
method_summary: Under an experienced guide (niryāpaka), the practitioner perfects faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity as death approaches, with confession, forgiveness, renunciation and meditation; it culminates in sallekhanā where the conditions hold (restricted: summary only).

warnings.text: To be undertaken only with the guide's supervision and when the body can no longer sustain the discipline; not from despair, desire for death, or desire for a reward.

name: Sallekhanā / santhārā (the canonical conditions)
method_summary: The gradual, voluntary giving up of food at the approach of an unavoidable death, with confession and meditation, under a teacher's guidance; the texts distinguish it from suicide by its conditions and state of mind (restricted: summary only, no procedure).

warnings.text: Only when the body can no longer sustain restraint (old age, incurable illness, famine, calamity); never out of passion, despair or wish for death.
One must not long for life or for death, nor wish for a reward (nidāna) in a future life.
It requires the permission and supervision of the teacher.

name: Atonement (prāyaścitta) in the Chedasūtras
method_summary: A mendicant who transgresses confesses to the teacher and receives an atonement fixed by the Chedasūtras according to the offence and the circumstances: confession, repentance, both, discarding, body-abandonment, fasts, reduction of seniority (cheda), re-initiation (mūla), suspension and expulsion (the Śvetāmbara tenfold list; the Digambara ninefold list differs).

name: The twelve special vows of the monk (bhikṣu-pratimā)
method_summary: A series of twelve progressively severe undertakings for qualified monks, restricting alms to one or a few 'portions' of food and drink for a month or more at a time and ending in intense night-long standing meditation (restricted: prolonged fasting — summary only).

warnings.text: Only for monks of sufficient bodily strength, scriptural learning and years of standing, with the teacher's permission.

name: The eleven stages of the layperson (upāsaka-pratimā)
method_summary: A layperson ascends through eleven stages of increasing renunciation — from right faith and the vows, through regular equanimity and holy-day fasts, to renouncing living food, household undertakings and food prepared for oneself — ending by living almost like a mendicant.

name: The Navapada Olī (āyambil fast)
method_summary: Twice a year for nine days Mūrtipūjaka laity worship the Siddhacakra of the nine 'stations' (the five supreme beings and right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity) and eat once a day a single bland, unspiced meal without oil, milk products or sweets (āyambil).

warnings.text: Fasts are to be undertaken according to one's strength (śaktitaḥ tapaḥ).

name: Worship of the Siddhacakra
method_summary: Worship of a diagram (yantra) of nine stations — Arhat, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu, and right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity — especially during the Navapada Olī; its legend is the story of Śrīpāla and Mayaṇāsundarī.

name: The year-long fast (varṣī-tapa)
method_summary: In memory of Ṛṣabha's long fast, a practitioner alternates fasting days and eating days for about a year, ending on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā with sugarcane juice (restricted: prolonged fasting — summary and warnings only).

warnings.text: Austerity is to be undertaken according to one's strength; fasting for fame or reward (nidāna) is faulty.

name: Upadhāna
method_summary: A period of several weeks during which laypeople live like mendicants under a teacher, fasting on alternate days and studying the liturgical sūtras, after which they are formally entitled to recite them (restricted in its fasting component: summary only).

name: Consecration of an image (pañcakalyāṇaka-pratiṣṭhā)
method_summary: A new image is consecrated by a festival re-enacting the five auspicious events of a Tīrthaṅkara's life — conception, birth (with the bath on Meru), renunciation, omniscience (the samavasaraṇa) and nirvāṇa — after which it is installed as the Jina.

name: The great head-anointing of Bāhubali
method_summary: About every twelve years the 58-foot image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is anointed from a scaffold with water, milk, sugarcane juice, sandal, saffron and other substances, in memory of his renunciation and standing meditation.

name: Pilgrimage to the tīrthas
method_summary: Pilgrimage on foot to the places of the kalyāṇakas and nirvāṇas and to great temple-hills — Sammeda Śikhara (Pārasnāth), Śatruñjaya (Pālitāṇā), Girnār, Pāvāpurī, Aṣṭāpada (in memory), Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Ābu, Rāṇakpur — often with vows and fasting; the 'six-rule' (cha'rī pālit) sangha pilgrimage imitates mendicant discipline.

equivalents.note: pilgrimage to sacred places in the Vedic traditions

name: Veneration of scripture (Jñāna Pañcamī / Śruta Pañcamī)
method_summary: Once a year manuscripts and books are cleaned, displayed and worshipped: Śvetāmbaras on the fifth of bright Kārttika (Jñāna Pañcamī), Digambaras on the fifth of bright Jyeṣṭha (Śruta Pañcamī), the day the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama was completed and worshipped.

name: Śruta Pañcamī (Digambara)
method_summary: The Digambara festival of scripture on the fifth of bright Jyeṣṭha, commemorating the completion of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama by Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali and the saṅgha's worship of the book.

equivalents.note: the Śvetāmbara scripture festival on another date

name: Dīvālī as Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa
method_summary: Jains keep Dīvālī as the night of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa at Pāvā, when the eighteen kings lit lamps 'since the light of knowledge is gone'; the next morning Gautama's omniscience is celebrated and the Jain new year (Vīra era) begins.

name: Akṣaya Tṛtīyā (Ṛṣabha's first alms)
method_summary: Commemorates the day Prince Śreyāṃsa offered sugarcane juice to Ṛṣabha, ending his long fast — the first alms of this era; those completing the year-long fast break it on this day.

name: Mahāvīra Jayantī
method_summary: The celebration of Mahāvīra's birth on the thirteenth of bright Caitra, with processions, worship and readings.

name: Maryādā Mahotsava (Terāpanth)
method_summary: The annual festival of the order's written code, instituted by Jayācārya, at which the ācārya assigns the monks' and nuns' travels for the year and the code is recited.

name: The Aṇuvrata movement
method_summary: Ācārya Tulsī's movement (1949) offering 'small vows' of non-violence, honesty and restraint to people of any religion, adapted from the lay vows.

name: Wearing the mouth-cloth
method_summary: Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī mendicants keep a cloth tied over the mouth at all times, and laypeople during equanimity practice, so that breath and speech do not harm the beings of the air.
